# What is location optimization?

##

::: {.focus-list}
- If I'm closing one service, which should it be?
- If I'm adding a new site to an existing service, which of these 5 possible places should I put it?
- If I'm spinning up a totally new service, how should I distribute my sites?
:::

# The Current (Python) Landscape

## [spopt](https://pysal.org/spopt/)

<br/>

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width='50%'}
### Pros

:::{.focus-list}
- Part of a wider ecosystem ([pysal](https://pysal.org/) - **P**ython **S**patial **A**nalysis **L**ibrary)
- 350+ github stars
- 24 contributors (i.e. pretty robust)
- Quite a lot of documentation...
:::

:::

::: {.column width='50%'}

:::{.focus-list}
- ... but the documentation is (imo) quite confusing
- Not healthcare or UK focussed
- Linear optimization returns a single option by default
- Need to manually create your own output plots
:::

:::

::::

## [HSMA](https://hsma.co.uk/hsma_content/modules/current_module_details/3_geographic_modelling_visualisation.html) and [Open Source Exeter MSc content](https://github.com/health-data-science-OR/healthcare-logistics/tree/master/optimisation)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width='50%'}
### Pros

:::{.focus-list}
- Returns multiple options
- Written with UK healthcare in mind
:::

:::

::: {.column width='50%'}

### Cons

:::{.focus-list}
- Requires manual copying and adapting of code
- Still need to manually create your own plots
- Risk of more errors due to unreviewed code without automated tests
- Still lots of repetition across organisations
:::

:::

::::


## lokigi

Lokigi is a brand new package building on the HSMA and Exeter approach.

It aims to provide an easy-to-use workflow to simplify and speed up location optimization work.


::: {.fragment}

The goal is to make it **work optimally for UK healthcare contexts**.

If it works for other contexts, it's a bonus - not the other way around.

:::


## Simple Problem Formulation

At its core, you only need a travel matrix.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hsma-tools/lokigi/refs/heads/main/sample_data/devon_miu_travel_matrix.csv")
from IPython.display import HTML
HTML(df.head(5).to_html(classes="styled-table", index=False))
```

---

Setting up your problem is easy.

```{python}
from lokigi.site import SiteProblem

problem = SiteProblem()

problem.add_travel_matrix(
    travel_matrix_df="https://github.com/hsma-tools/lokigi/blob/main/sample_data/devon_miu_travel_matrix.csv",
    source_col="from_id",
    unit="minutes",
    )

```

<br/>

And you can solve it with a single command.

```{python}
solution = problem.solve(p=4)
```

---

By default, lokigi will

- brute force the solution
- assume you want to solve a p-median problem (minimize travel time - weighted by demand if you provide that)

::: {.fragment}
It also supports

- p-center (minimizing max travel time)
- the Maximal Covering Location Problem (optimizing for being within x distance)
:::


::: {.fragment}
Greedy and GRASP allow solving of problems that are too big to brute force
:::


---

You can then see a range of metrics for all possible solutions.

```{python}
#| eval: false
solution.show_solutions()
```


```{python}
#| echo: false
HTML(solution.show_solutions()
  [['solution_rank','site_indices','unweighted_average','90th_percentile','max']]
  .head(4).to_html(classes="styled-table", index=False)
  )
```

<br/>

The full solution table also includes site names and the underlying per-region dataframe for every evaluated combination.

---

And we can output plots.

```{python}
solution.plot_n_best_combinations_bar(n_best=5, interactive=False, static_width=15)
```

---

By adding more data, you can plot your solutions too.

```{python}
problem.add_sites(
    "https://github.com/hsma-tools/lokigi/blob/main/sample_data/devon_mius.geojson",
    candidate_id_col="Facility_Name"
    )
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
HTML(problem.show_sites()[['Facility_Name','Latitude','Longitude']].head(5).to_html(classes="styled-table", index=False))
```

---


```{python}
problem.plot_sites(interactive=True)
```

---

You can load in easy-to-find LSOA/MSOA/other UK geometry files...

```{python}
problem.add_region_geometry_layer(
    "https://github.com/hsma-programme/h6_3c_interactive_plots_travel/raw/main/h6_3c_interactive_plots_travel/example_code/LSOA_2011_Boundaries_Super_Generalised_Clipped_BSC_EW_V4.geojson",
    common_col="LSOA11NM"
    )
```

<br/>

The [government geoportal (geoportal.statistics.gov.uk/)](https://geoportal.statistics.gov.uk/) has everything you need

---

And optionally we can add demand data too if we want to weight our solution.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import numpy as np
demand_df = problem.show_travel_matrix()[["from_id"]].copy()
np.random.seed(42)
demand_df["demand"] = np.random.randint(50, 351, size=len(df))
demand_df = demand_df.rename(columns={"from_id": "source"})

problem.add_demand(
    demand_df,
    demand_col="demand",
    location_id_col="source"
    )
```

```{python}
#| eval: false
problem.add_demand(
    "datasets/devon_miu_demand.csv", # Local files supported too!
    demand_col="demand",
    location_id_col="source"
    )

problem.show_demand()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
HTML(problem.show_demand().head(5).to_html(classes="styled-table", index=False))
```

---

We can inspect this data, with joins to all the other data in our problem being handled automatically.

```{python}
problem.plot_region_geometry_layer(plot_demand=True, interactive=True)
```

---

We simply solve again!

This time we'll also pass in how many regions we want to be within a given travel time.

```{python}
solution = problem.solve(p=4, threshold_for_coverage=20)
```

(enhancements to this coming soon - i.e. counting based on demand/population, not per-region)

---

And then we can plot any given solution...

```{python}
solution.plot_best_combination()
```

---

As well as the sites people are nearest to...

```{python}
solution.plot_best_combination(plot_site_allocation=True)
```

---

And the coverage.

```{python}
solution.plot_best_combination(plot_regions_not_meeting_threshold=True)
```

---

Or multiple solutions at once.

```{python}
solution.plot_n_best_combinations(n_best=3);
```

---

We also get plots like this, helping us to understand tradeoffs.

```{python}
solution.plot_simple_pareto_front()
```

## Additional Features - Equity

We recognise that the equity of solutions is important, so there are some early functions to help assess this.

This is again designed to work with easily available government equity data from sources like the ONS geoportal again.

```{python}
problem.add_equity_data(
    "https://github.com/hsma-tools/lokigi/blob/main/sample_data/Index_of_Multiple_Deprivation_(Dec_2015)_Lookup_in_England.csv",
    equity_col="IMD15",
    common_col="LSOA11NM",
    label="Indices of Multiple Deprivation",
    continuous_measure=True,
    reverse=False
    )

solution = problem.solve(p=4, threshold_for_coverage=20)
```

---

And enables plots like this

```{python}
solution.check_solution_equity(return_plot=True, interactive=False, colour_mode="above_below_avg");
```

---

Comparison of equity across multiple solutions

```{python}
solution.plot_top_n_solution_equity(cols=2, n=2, colour_mode="above_below_avg");
```

---

And equity maps.

```{python}
groupings = {
    "IMD15 Highest Deprivation": [1, 2, 3], "IMD15 Mid": [4, 5, 6, 7],
    "IMD15 Lowest Deprivation": [8, 9, 10],
}
solution.plot_combination_by_equity(groupings=groupings, figsize_multiplier=7, ncols=3);
```

You can currently also produce a few plots and metrics to compare two solution sets.

## Key questions

:::{.incremental}
- Does this actually feel useful? Are we providing tools to answer the right kind of questions?
- What key features are missing that would stop you from using it in its current state?
- How much support/help do we need to provide for travel time matrix generation? Currently has example in docs, but no helper methods.
- Is there a 'ready-to-use' report format we could export? Is this useful?
- What about a web-based tool so people don't have to write code?
- Do we need to look at CO2 emissions? (but could basically optimize on it already)
- What else am I missing about these problems on the ground?
:::
